changes: When a new version is announced but its download has not finished publishing, the game now says so and suggests trying again shortly, instead of reporting that an update package was not found. That message appeared for a short while after every release and read like a fault in the game when nothing was wrong.
Rewrote bot driving behavior. Bots learn how to use brakes when necessary, slow down or accelerate based on incoming turns, avoid obstacles, and hard difficulty mode is a serious hard mode now.
Fixed a long-standing bug where when another vehicle crosses the finish line, the player would only hear it's sound and the sound would get cut completely instead of slowing down.
serverChanges: Fork test build carrying the renamed, self-replacing updater. Updating to it from an earlier fork build is the migration: the old Updater runs once more and brings TopSpeedUpdater in. The update after this one is the first done by TopSpeedUpdater, replacing files by rename.

Running the server program again from a folder that already has a server running now opens a console onto the one that is running, instead of starting a second server that quietly claims the same ports. Everything the running server prints appears in the new window, commands typed there are answered by it, and typing exit leaves the server running. Only one window at a time may hold the console: any other copy is told so the moment it connects, and when the window holding it closes, however it closes, the next to arrive takes its place.

The server can now be installed as a system service, so it starts with the machine and keeps running when nobody is logged in. Type service for a menu, or add the verb to skip it: service install, uninstall, start, stop, restart or status. The same actions are available as command line options, so nothing has to be typed into a running server. Each folder gets its own service, worked out from where the server lives, so two servers on one machine can both be installed without naming either.

On Windows the service runs as NT AUTHORITY\LocalService, never as you and never as an administrator, and is granted permission to write inside the server folder only, which is what lets it update itself. It starts with the machine rather than two minutes after it. Installing asks for administrator rights through the ordinary prompt; nothing here ever asks for a password.

On Linux and macOS the service is installed with sudo ./TopSpeed.Server --install-service, which writes the systemd unit or launchd job where the system keeps them, loads it, and reports what it registered. It is registered to run as the account that owns the server folder, which is you and not root, and that holds however you became root: su works as well as sudo, so a machine set up without sudo is installable too. Where root is the only account, as on many rented servers and in containers, root is accepted. Run any service command without root and it tells you the command to run, with the full path already filled in.

On Linux, service status says whether the service is installed, running and set to start with the machine, without needing root, and any other service command typed without root reports that first. On macOS reading that needs root, so the server says which command reports it.

Starting or restarting the service from a window attached to a running server hands the folder over rather than refusing: the running server stops, the service starts, and the same window attaches to the service.

On Linux and macOS the server refuses to run as root where the folder belongs to somebody else. A server run that way wrote its settings, its log and its own updates into the folder as root, which the folder's owner could not later replace; nothing said so at the time, and it surfaced as an update that would not install. Where root owns the folder nothing is refused.

Replaced the "Check for updates on startup" switch with an "Update checking" setting offering three choices: off never checks, notify says when a new version is available and leaves the decision to you, and auto installs new versions by itself. Servers that had the old switch on become notify, and those that had it off become off. The server now starts first and checks afterwards, so a server launched with its window hidden no longer looks as though it is running while nobody can connect.

Approving an update is no longer a yes or no question. Typing update shows what has changed and says what to type next; typing update again approves it. If players are connected, the install waits for the last of them to leave and says how many are on; update typed again meanwhile reports what is scheduled rather than starting anything else, and update --force installs at once, disconnecting anyone still connected. An approval survives the daily check finding the same version, an offer nobody approved expires after a day, and nothing installs because of a single mistyped word.

A server you started yourself on Linux or macOS updates in the window you were already using and comes back in it, with the updater's own output shown while it works, however many times it updates. On Windows the updated server opens in a new console window and the original returns to its prompt, which the guide explains; a service is the better answer there for a server nobody wants to watch.

A window attached to a server follows it through an update. On Linux and macOS it says the server is updating, waits, and attaches again by itself a couple of seconds after the server is back, as the updated program. On Windows it says the server is updating and closes, because the files being replaced are the ones it is running from; run the program again once the update is done.

A server running as a service installs updates and is back within seconds. On Windows the update is no longer reported to the service manager as a crash, so a stop that was meant stays stopped; on Linux and macOS the unit waits for the update itself rather than pausing for two minutes to cover it. Everything that waits for an update to finish now waits the same five minutes before treating it as abandoned.

Running the server program while an update is being installed says so and stops, instead of starting a second server into the folder the updater is still writing. A folder holding parts of two versions says so at startup. A version that was installed but came back reporting the old one is not installed again by itself, and the server does not check again in the first minutes after installing one.

A new version whose download has not been published yet is treated as something to retry rather than an error: the server checks again after twenty minutes, then forty, then hourly, says so when it first notices and once more after the second attempt, and gives up after a day. Downloads are checked against their expected size, an incomplete one is reported and removed rather than handed to the updater, and approving an update fetches it exactly once.

Added a "Log file" setting and a "Log level" setting. Logging is off by default; a file name or path turns it on, a relative one lands beside the server, and the level uses the same words as the --log-level option. The log can be read while the server is running, update messages on the console are timestamped, and the update check leaves a line at debug level saying what it found. A server with no console reports a download's progress every quarter rather than every percent.

The updater now replaces each file by writing the new one beside it and renaming it into place, rather than rewriting the old file where it stands. macOS refuses to run a program that has been run and then rewritten in place, however correct its new contents, which could leave a Mac server unable to start after an update with every file in order; and a file rewritten under a program still using it could crash that program on Linux. The updater also replaces itself the same way, so it is no longer frozen at whichever version first arrived in a folder, and it now ships as TopSpeedUpdater; a folder that still has the old Updater uses it for one more update, which brings the new one in, and the old one is then removed.
The server's window is named after what it is doing, such as "TopSpeed Server, port 28630", with "attached" added for a window attached to one, so two servers on one machine can be told apart.

Start Server.command on macOS and start-server.sh on Linux ship in the download for starting the server from a file manager, and the guide says what opening TopSpeed.Server itself does there instead. The guide also covers getting the server onto a Mac past quarantine, and every command it tells you to run is kept out of the translated text so a translation cannot change what you are told to type.
